card.label: Foundation species
card.learning_takeaway: Connect habitat structure supplied by organisms with the communities that depend on it.
card.card: Foundation species help build the physical setting of a community. Kelp forms underwater forests, while reef-building corals create habitats used by many other organisms. Their importance comes from shaping the environment that supports the community, rather than simply being another species within it.

evidence.note: OpenStax’s Foundation Species passage identifies kelp forests and coral habitat construction as community-shaping examples.

relations.note: Habitat construction by foundation species can be compared with ecosystem engineering, while avoiding an assertion that the two categories are identical.

card.label: Variable-rate irrigation
card.learning_takeaway: Match irrigation amounts to different areas of a field instead of assuming every area needs the same water.
card.card: Variable-rate irrigation changes water delivery across different parts of a field. Control zones and prescription maps can account for meaningful differences in soil or crop demand. The technology answers where and how much to apply; its advantage is limited when a field has little relevant variation.

evidence.note: UMN describes zone control, prescription maps and reduced benefit in sufficiently uniform fields.

relations.note: Spatially varied application is a specific control approach within irrigation rather than a second identity for irrigation as a whole.

card.label: Mauna Loa Observatory
card.learning_takeaway: See how representative air sampling and repeated calibration support an atmospheric CO2 record.
card.card: Mauna Loa Observatory’s carbon-dioxide record depends on more than taking repeated readings. Air samples are assessed for background conditions, and the analyzer is frequently checked against reference gases. Reporting carbon dioxide in dry air helps prevent changing water vapor from masquerading as a change in carbon dioxide.

evidence.note: NOAA explains background selection, frequent calibration and why dry-air mole fraction removes dilution effects of variable water vapor.

relations.note: Mauna Loa and Landsat offer different long-term environmental records whose comparability depends on calibration, an editorial measurement-practice bridge.

card.label: Convergent evolution
card.learning_takeaway: Explain similar functions that evolved separately rather than being inherited from a shared ancestor.
card.card: Convergent evolution produces similar features in separate evolutionary lineages. Bird and bat wings both serve flight, but their wing structures arose independently. Their underlying forelimbs still share ancestry, showing that the answer depends on which feature and evolutionary level a comparison is examining.

evidence.note: Berkeley connects analogous wings with convergent evolution while distinguishing homologous forelimbs.

relations.note: Contrasting wing function with forelimb ancestry makes convergence and biological homology distinguishable without making them mutually exclusive at every level.

card.label: Mortise-and-tenon joint
card.learning_takeaway: Connect a fitted projection, its matching recess and seated shoulders with a strong wooden joint.
card.card: A mortise-and-tenon joint fits a projecting end of one piece into a matching recess in another. Close-fitting faces provide contact for bonding, while the shoulders seat against the receiving piece. The arrangement connects shape and fit with joint performance, rather than relying on an end-to-end butt connection alone.

evidence.note: The original WOOD instruction defines projection/recess, glue surface and shoulder contact as components of the fitted joint.

relations.note: This is a specific geometric method of joining wooden components within woodworking.

card.label: Egg protein coagulation
card.learning_takeaway: Explain why a liquid egg becomes a network that traps water as it is heated.
card.card: Heating egg white unfolds proteins and allows them to connect with one another. The resulting network traps water, changing a flowing liquid into a firmer structure. Too much heating can make that network rubbery, showing how the same molecular process can produce very different cooking textures.

evidence.note: Exploratorium describes heat unfolding egg-white proteins, intermolecular bonds, trapped water and rubberiness after excessive heating.

relations.note: Eggs can stabilize food in different ways: heat-linked protein networks versus yolk emulsifiers separating fat droplets.

card.label: Mulching
card.learning_takeaway: Explain how a surface covering changes evaporation, weed growth and soil temperature.
card.card: Mulching covers the soil surface with a chosen material. The layer can slow evaporation, reduce light available to weeds and alter soil temperature. Those effects depend on the material, so a gardener’s choice of covering changes more than the appearance of the bed.

evidence.note: UMN explains surface cover, moisture conservation, weed-light restriction and material-dependent thermal effects.

relations.note: A mulch layer is a specific gardening intervention affecting root-zone conditions.

card.label: Understitching
card.learning_takeaway: Keep a facing from rolling to the garment’s outside by securing its seam allowance to the facing.
card.card: Understitching secures a seam allowance to the facing on the inside of a garment. This encourages the seam to roll inward and helps prevent the facing from showing on the outside. It controls an already assembled edge, rather than stabilizing a loose pattern piece before sewing.

evidence.locator: Seam-allowance understitching; Tips for Applying Facings
evidence.note: NMSU describes pressing the allowance toward the facing, understitching and preventing the facing from rolling outside.

relations.note: These stitching operations differ in timing and purpose: control of an assembled facing versus stabilization of an unjoined cut edge.

card.label: Scribing to fit
card.learning_takeaway: Fit a new component to an irregular existing surface by transferring its contour onto the workpiece.
card.card: Scribing to fit transfers the contour of an existing surface onto a new workpiece. A cabinet panel beside an uneven wall, for example, can be marked to match that wall’s profile. The method handles irregularity directly instead of assuming that every surrounding surface is straight.

evidence.locator: Transferring wall contours onto a panel
evidence.note: Lee Valley describes transferring contours and specifically copying an old irregular wall profile onto a cabinet panel.

relations.note: The contrast separates copying an encountered contour from reusing dimensions already stored on a story stick.

card.label: Swarna-Sub1
card.learning_takeaway: See flood tolerance as a bounded crop trait rather than an ability to survive indefinitely underwater.
card.card: Swarna-Sub1 adds temporary flood tolerance to a widely grown rice variety through the SUB1 breeding trait. It can survive periods of submergence that threaten ordinary crops, but longer floods still pose serious limits. The case shows why a tolerant variety is not an invulnerable one.

evidence.note: IRRI names Swarna-Sub1 and describes SUB1-enabled temporary submergence survival with sharply reduced performance in longer floods.

relations.note: The two named rice varieties illustrate different breeding objectives: semidwarf crop architecture and temporary flood tolerance.

card.label: Karner blue butterfly
card.learning_takeaway: Explore how ant attendance can protect butterfly larvae while the ants receive carbohydrate-rich secretions.
card.card: Karner blue butterfly larvae can exchange a sugary secretion for protection from ants. The ants gain food, while their attendance can reduce threats to the caterpillars. This butterfly offers a concrete example of mutualism, with the particular ant partners varying between locations.

evidence.note: The community-ecology passage describes carbohydrate-rich larval secretions, ant protection and variation in attending ant species.

relations.note: The documented food-for-protection exchange illustrates mutualism in this named butterfly.

card.label: Endosymbiotic theory
card.learning_takeaway: Use organelle genomes, division and membranes as evidence of ancestry from once-independent cells.
card.card: Mitochondria retain their own genetic material, divide in a bacteria-like way and have surrounding membranes consistent with an engulfed ancestor. These clues support endosymbiotic origins from once-independent cells. The broad ancestry is well supported even while details of the earliest host–partner sequence remain debated.

evidence.note: OpenStax discusses mitochondrial genomes, fission-like division, membranes and unresolved ordering relative to the host nucleus.

relations.note: Organelle similarities and shared ancestry offer a molecular/cellular setting for the ancestry reasoning introduced by biological homology.

card.label: Turbidity
card.learning_takeaway: Connect suspended matter with light scattering, absorption and reduced underwater visibility.
card.card: Turbidity describes water cloudiness associated with suspended particles and other material that interferes with light. Sediment or algae can reduce visibility and the light reaching underwater plants. Cloudy water is not automatically polluted, since some waters are naturally turbid, but the change can still matter ecologically.

evidence.note: EPA’s clarity account links suspended matter/algae, lower visibility and light available to aquatic plants, including naturally turbid waters.

relations.note: A Secchi disk provides a visual clarity assessment, while turbidity describes the clouding property influencing underwater light.

card.label: Healthy-volunteer bias in screening studies
card.learning_takeaway: Explain why screened and unscreened groups can differ in outcomes for reasons unrelated to the screening.
card.card: People who choose to participate in screening may differ from those who do not, including in health behaviors and other risks. Better outcomes in volunteers can therefore reflect those starting differences. Healthy-volunteer bias makes a simple screened-versus-unscreened comparison an unreliable measure of the screening’s effect.

evidence.note: NCI’s study-design discussion identifies self-selected participants’ different health behavior and lower unrelated mortality as a screening-evaluation concern.

relations.note: A randomized comparison can address initial selection differences that a simple volunteer/nonvolunteer contrast cannot, though later participation and follow-up still matter.

card.label: Renal countercurrent multiplication
card.learning_takeaway: Explain how opposite flows and unequal permeability build a medullary concentration gradient.
card.card: Fluid travels in opposite directions through neighboring limbs of the kidney’s loop of Henle. The descending limb allows water to leave, while the thick ascending limb moves salt outward without water following. These differences help build the medullary concentration gradient used to recover water.

evidence.locator: Descending Loop; Ascending Loop; Countercurrent Multiplier System
evidence.note: The descending/thick-ascending passages support unequal water permeability, active salt reabsorption and the opposing-flow arrangement.

relations.note: The gradient-building arrangement supports the water recovery that ADH-regulated collecting-duct channels permit.

card.label: Elwha River restoration
card.learning_takeaway: Explore how removing dams reconnects fish migration and sediment movement.
card.card: Removing dams from the Elwha River restored connections between upstream habitat and the sea. The project reopened routes used by migrating fish and allowed sediment to move again. It demonstrates that river restoration can involve reconnecting processes across a whole watershed, not only repairing one riverbank.

evidence.note: NPS describes the dams’ barriers to fish and sediment and the restoration through dam removal.

relations.note: Reconnecting fish movement and sediment transport makes the Elwha project an ecological case linking organisms with physical processes.

card.label: Coral bleaching
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish stress-driven loss of symbiotic algae from immediate coral death.
card.card: Stressed corals can lose the symbiotic algae living in their tissues, leaving them pale or white. This bleaching also removes an important food source. A bleached coral is not necessarily dead, but prolonged stress makes recovery harder and can ultimately lead to death.

evidence.note: NOAA explains stress-driven expulsion of symbiotic algae, loss of color and food, possible recovery and death if stress persists.

relations.note: Bleaching shows what can happen when a coral’s beneficial partnership with algae is disrupted.

card.label: Lake-effect snow
card.learning_takeaway: Trace narrow snow bands to cold air gaining heat and moisture over unfrozen lake water.
card.card: Cold air moving across a warmer, unfrozen lake gains heat and moisture. As that air rises, narrow cloud bands can form and deliver lake-effect snow downwind. Wind direction strongly affects where the snow falls, so heavy snowfall can occur close to places receiving very little.

evidence.note: NWS describes heat/moisture transfer over unfrozen Great Lakes, rising air, narrow snow bands and strong wind-direction dependence.

relations.note: These are different routes to precipitation: local moisture uptake over a lake versus concentrated long-distance vapor transport.

card.label: Homology (biology)
card.learning_takeaway: Identify similarity inherited from common ancestry, even when present-day functions differ.
card.card: In biology, homologous features resemble one another because they descend from a shared ancestral feature. Bird and bat forelimbs are homologous, even though their wings evolved separately as flight structures. The comparison shows why common ancestry and similarity of present-day function must be distinguished.

evidence.note: Berkeley explicitly treats bird/bat forelimbs as homologous and their wings as independently evolved analogous flight structures.

relations.note: The same bird–bat comparison separates common-ancestry resemblance from independently evolved similarity in flight.

card.label: Enzymatic browning
card.learning_takeaway: Connect a cut fruit surface, oxygen and enzyme activity with a change in color.
card.card: Cutting an apple exposes its tissues to oxygen, allowing enzymes to drive browning reactions. Changing conditions such as acidity can slow the process. The color change therefore connects damage to plant cells with chemical activity, rather than being explained solely by the fruit drying out.

evidence.note: ACS’s explanatory section connects exposed apple tissue, oxygen, enzymes and the slowing effect of acidity.

relations.note: Both topics concern food-quality changes mediated by enzymes, while acidifying an exposed surface and heat-blanching before freezing are different interventions.

card.label: Cascadia Subduction Zone
card.learning_takeaway: Explain the paired coastal and volcanic ranges produced by the descending Juan de Fuca Plate.
card.card: In the Cascadia Subduction Zone, the Juan de Fuca Plate descends beneath North America. Scraped-off material helps build coastal ranges, while deeper processes support the Cascade volcanic arc inland. The region shows how one convergent boundary can produce distinct landscape features at different distances.

evidence.note: NPS’s Cascadia section links the descending Juan de Fuca Plate, coastal accreted material and inland volcanic chain.

relations.note: Cascadia is a particular geographic example of the broader subduction process.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:fine_application_wording, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Crop rotation
card.learning_takeaway: Disrupt recurring crop-pest associations by changing the crop grown in a field over time.
card.card: Crop rotation changes the crops grown in a field through a planned sequence over time. This can interrupt recurring pest associations and diversify how the field is used. It is a preventive management practice, rather than simply moving an existing pest after it has become a problem.

evidence.note: Identifies crop rotation as a way to prevent pest problems within IPM.
Defines planned crop sequence over time on the same field and reduced pest pressure as a possible benefit.

relations.note: EPA explicitly includes rotation among preventive practices within integrated pest management.

card.label: Leather temper
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a hide’s pliability from its thickness when choosing between draping and shape-holding uses.
card.card: Leather temper describes how readily a hide bends, drapes or holds its shape. It is different from thickness: equally thick pieces can feel quite different. A soft garment panel and a firm structured bag may require different tempers, so flexing a sample reveals information a thickness measurement cannot.

evidence.locator: Definition; Matching temper to the job; Describing temper
evidence.note: United Leather distinguishes temper from thickness and relates soft/firm behavior to garment and structured-bag uses; Tandy independently defines pliability.
The independent supplier glossary defines temper as finished-leather pliability from stiff to supple.

relations.note: Temper is a particular mechanical property of finished leather, not a different material identity or simply its thickness.

card.label: Genetics
card.learning_takeaway: Connect inherited DNA variation with environmental influences rather than treating genes as destiny.
card.card: Genetics studies inheritance and variation, including how genes interact with the environment. A DNA difference can influence a trait without determining it alone. Studying genes alongside behavior and surroundings helps explain why genetic information is only part of the story of health.
card.original_description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

evidence.note: NHGRI defines inheritance, DNA variation and environmental interaction; its narration explicitly treats behavior and surroundings as additional health influences.

relations.note: Mosaicism extends the inheritance discussion to DNA differences arising after fertilization, showing why genetic variation need not be shared by every cell.

imported_records.description: Studying inheritance and variation in living organisms.

card.label: Arterial blood gas testing
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish blood oxygenation, carbon-dioxide removal and acid-base measurements in one arterial sample.
card.card: An arterial blood gas test analyzes a blood sample for oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH. These measurements address oxygenation, removal of carbon dioxide and acid–base balance together. Unlike a light-based pulse-oximeter reading, the test requires blood from an artery and supplies information beyond oxygen saturation.

evidence.locator: What is an arterial blood gas test?
evidence.note: Supports arterial blood sampling and the oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH measurements.
Supports the light-based, noninvasive oxygen-saturation comparison.

relations.note: An arterial sample can assess CO2 and pH alongside oxygen, whereas the optical method estimates saturation; the methods are not interchangeable.

card.label: F1 hybrid
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a deliberate parental cross from the variable offspring produced by saving seed from that hybrid.
card.card: An F1 hybrid is the first generation produced by crossing distinct parental lines. In crop varieties, that cross can combine useful traits, but saved seed from the hybrid need not reproduce the same combination. Later offspring can vary, even when the original hybrid plants seemed very consistent.
card.original_description: first-generation hybrid (or crossbreed) animal or plant

evidence.note: Verifies F1 as first filial generation from a cross of parental strains.
Supports combining traits of different parental varieties in crop hybrids.
Explicitly supports the variability of offspring grown from seed saved from F1 hybrids.

relations.note: A deliberate parental cross and variation in later generations provide a practical crop-breeding application of inheritance and variation.

imported_records.description: first-generation hybrid (or crossbreed) animal or plant

card.label: Oceanography
card.learning_takeaway: Connect ocean chemistry, life, seafloor history and water movement as interacting research areas.
card.card: Oceanography studies the ocean through its water movement, chemistry, living communities and seafloor history. These perspectives overlap: circulation can move nutrients that influence marine life. Field observations, experiments and models connect the ocean’s physical setting with the organisms and chemical processes operating within it.
card.original_description: Investigating the physical, chemical and biological properties of oceans.

evidence.note: Supports the field’s physical, chemical, biological and geological scope and research methods.
Supports the example connecting circulation, nutrients and marine productivity.

relations.note: Coastal upwelling illustrates how circulation delivers nutrients and connects physical with biological oceanography.

imported_records.description: Investigating the physical, chemical and biological properties of oceans.

card.label: Starch retrogradation
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish molecular re-ordering during storage from the initial swelling of starch during cooking.
card.card: After starch has been cooked, its molecules can associate again and develop more ordered structures during storage. This retrogradation changes the starch matrix and can affect texture and digestibility. It is a later rearrangement, distinct from the initial water uptake and swelling of heated starch granules.

evidence.note: Supports chain reassociation and ordering during storage and effects on structure and digestibility.
Supports initial water uptake/swelling during heating, used as the explicit comparison.

relations.note: The comparison separates initial heat-driven granule swelling from later chain reassociation.

card.label: Flat-felled seam
card.learning_takeaway: Create an enclosed-edge seam that is folded down and secured flat with visible stitching.
card.card: A flat-felled seam wraps one fabric edge within a folded edge and secures the assembly flat with stitching. The enclosed raw edges and additional stitching produce a durable finish familiar from jeans and other hard-wearing garments. Its flattened construction distinguishes it from a French seam’s enclosed ridge.

evidence.note: Supports folded enclosure, stitching flat, durability and jeans use.
Supports the contrast with enclosing one seam inside another.

relations.note: The connection compares two genuinely different enclosed-edge constructions rather than counting synonymous finishes.

card.label: Randomized controlled trial
card.learning_takeaway: Use chance-based assignment and a comparison group to assess an intervention’s effects.
card.card: A randomized controlled trial uses chance to assign participants to an intervention or comparison group. Comparing outcomes helps separate the intervention’s effects from differences that might influence who receives it. Randomization is a design tool; clear follow-up and careful analysis are still needed for a trustworthy result.

evidence.note: Supports chance assignment and comparing experimental and control outcomes.
Supports the qualification that randomization alone does not remove analysis or missing-outcome concerns.

relations.note: Concealing forthcoming assignments protects the random allocation process against selective enrollment.

card.label: International HapMap Project
card.learning_takeaway: See how patterns of co-inherited DNA variants helped connect genomic variation with disease.
card.card: The International HapMap Project charted common patterns of human DNA variation, especially groups of variants often inherited together. These genomic neighborhoods helped researchers connect variation with disease. Its contribution was a map of shared variation patterns, rather than merely another sequence from a single individual.

evidence.note: NHGRI identifies the project, co-inherited haplotypes, common human variation and the use of linkage-disequilibrium patterns in disease studies.

relations.note: HapMap’s co-inherited variant neighborhoods give a named research example of genomic linkage patterns; the project is not the general linkage mechanism.

card.label: E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment
card.learning_takeaway: See how revived archived populations let researchers test whether prior mutations enabled a later innovation.
card.card: In the E. coli Long-Term Evolution Experiment, researchers replayed evolution using bacteria from different points in one population’s history. Later samples were more likely to evolve citrate use. The result showed how earlier genetic changes could enable a later innovation, making evolutionary history experimentally testable.

evidence.note: The 2008 primary abstract reports replay experiments from different generations and a higher probability of citrate use in later clones, supporting historical contingency.

relations.note: Replaying different inherited genetic backgrounds links this experiment to genetics through the effect of prior changes on a later trait.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Broadbalk Wheat Experiment
card.learning_takeaway: Use a persistent untreated comparison to interpret crop responses to fertilizer over many years.
card.card: Broadbalk compares wheat grown under different nutrient treatments across many years. An unfertilized strip maintained since 1843 provides a persistent reference against which fertilized plots can be read. The experiment shows how a long-lived control helps separate treatment effects from the changing background of agricultural seasons.

evidence.note: Rothamsted states the nutrient-treatment purpose and unfertilized control strip maintained since 1843.

relations.note: Broadbalk and Park Grass are separate long-term Rothamsted experiments, useful for comparing arable nutrient studies with permanent-grassland treatment histories.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Park Grass Experiment
card.learning_takeaway: Interpret a long-term grassland experiment in light of treatment design and changes in measurement methods.
card.card: Park Grass has studied grassland responses to fertilizer and liming since the nineteenth century. Its long record is not a single unchanging protocol: later liming subplots and changes in harvesting affect comparisons. Reading the experiment requires the treatment and measurement history alongside the hay-yield numbers.

evidence.locator: Study description; Liming design; Harvest methods
evidence.note: The e-RA dataset describes the experiment’s 1856 origin, 1965 liming subplots, hay yields and historical harvesting changes affecting comparability.

relations.note: Both experiments offer long records, but the inspected Park Grass design is a distinct grassland/liming study rather than another name for Broadbalk wheat plots.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: ENCODE
card.learning_takeaway: Distinguish identifying functional genomic elements from merely obtaining a DNA sequence.
card.card: ENCODE, the Encyclopedia of DNA Elements, investigates the working parts of the genome. Its research includes epigenomic maps from different cell types, helping distinguish the DNA sequence a cell carries from the regions it uses. A shared genome can support different cellular patterns of activity.

evidence.locator: How are researchers exploring the epigenome?
evidence.note: NHGRI states that ENCODE catalogs working genomic parts and includes cell-type epigenomic maps; the same fact sheet explains differentiated cells and altered marks.

relations.note: Histone marks are one kind of epigenomic information that makes ENCODE’s cell-type maps useful for studying differential genome use.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Isle Royale
card.learning_takeaway: Use an isolated island study to distinguish predator effects from climate, disease and food availability.
card.card: On Isle Royale in Lake Superior, a long-running study follows wolves, moose and their environment. Predator numbers matter, but disease, climate and available food also influence population changes. The island illustrates why a predator–prey relationship cannot be understood from two population counts alone.

evidence.locator: Why is Isle Royale a Unique Research Location?; Predator-Prey Relationships
evidence.note: NPS locates the island in Lake Superior and documents the long-running study, disease effects and changing roles of climate and forage.

relations.note: The island study demonstrates ecology’s need to consider interacting predators, prey and environmental conditions.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Maydianne Andrade
card.learning_takeaway: See how competing explanations for redback mating behavior can be tested with observations and experiments.
card.card: Maydianne Andrade investigated why male redback spiders sometimes risk being eaten during mating. Her observations and experiments compared nutritional, remating and paternity explanations. The case shows how an apparently self-defeating behavior can be studied by separating competing hypotheses and measuring reproductive consequences.

evidence.note: Berkeley’s teaching case names Andrade, lays out the three hypotheses and describes observations and laboratory experiments.

relations.note: Andrade’s named research program supplies the experiments used to study the redback sexual-cannibalism case.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:named_subject, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Framingham Heart Study
card.learning_takeaway: See how repeated examinations across generations established patterns of cardiovascular risk.
card.card: The Framingham Heart Study follows community participants over time, with repeated examinations and later generations joining the research. It connected factors such as blood pressure and cholesterol with future cardiovascular disease. Its long view shows how risk can be studied before illness becomes apparent.

evidence.note: NHLBI describes repeated cohort examinations, multigenerational participation and identification of cardiovascular risk factors including pressure and cholesterol.

relations.note: Population follow-up can identify prevention targets, linking this specific study with public health’s community-level focus.

card.label: Steam bending
card.learning_takeaway: Use heat and moisture to soften wood, then retain a curved shape while it cools and dries.
card.card: Steam bending uses heat and moisture to make suitable wood more flexible. The piece is shaped and then restrained while it cools and dries, helping it retain the curve. Moisture changes later can still alter that shape, so bending success involves both forming and conditioning the material.

evidence.locator: Principles of Plasticizing and Bending; Fixing the Bend
evidence.note: USDA Chapter 19 describes heat/moisture plasticization, restraint during cooling/drying and later moisture-dependent curvature changes.

relations.note: Steam bending is a wood-shaping process whose success depends on the material’s moisture and heat response.

sample.selection_reason: Purposive coverage/risk selection: risk:editorial_relationship, risk:fine_application_wording, risk:qualification_or_assumption

card.label: Bias facings
card.learning_takeaway: Finish a curved fabric edge using a narrow strip whose bias orientation allows it to conform to the curve.
card.card: A bias facing uses a narrow strip of fabric cut on the bias to finish a curved edge. The strip can be shaped to follow the curve without the bulk of a wider facing. Its usefulness comes from how the fabric direction allows the finish to conform.

evidence.note: NMSU describes narrow bias strips shaped to curves and their use to reduce visible or heavy facings.

relations.note: A bias facing is a specific sewn curved-edge finish within garment construction.
